Many people may not know this, but the Senate right now has something called culture, right? where you can't even get a bill heard or at least voted on until you have at least 60 members of the Senate, which will close the debate. That's called cloture. So, yes, did we have majority in the Senate the last two years before this last election? Yes, but we did not have that 60 votes necessary to close the debate and actually have a vote. And so we had the majority, the simple majority, but unfortunately the existing rules of the Senate, we can have a simple majority of the Senate and the House and still not be able to get anything done because you've got at least 41 members of the Senate who refuse to allow a vote on an issue. So yes, but this issue has been kind of a political football that both parties have probably, frankly, kicked back and forth. Yeah. So I think certainly from the conservative standpoint, the Republican caucus standpoint, The first thing, not negotiable, I think we have to have to solve first, is we've got to have border integrity. Because it doesn't matter what other rules and laws we have, if there's no way for us to enforce our boundaries and our borders, we don't have sovereignty. And so I think the first thing we have to do is to protect the southern border. We have to have a process whereby legal immigration takes place. And that legal immigration has to provide a reasonable in terms of a timeframe, a reasonable process for individuals to apply for citizenship and become citizens. I think it also has to be merit-based. I don't agree with the lottery system. I think we have the right as a nation to determine what are the specific individuals in terms of their expertise and their skill and whatnot to come into the nation. We've always done that in the past and I think that's probably what we need to get back to. I don't believe in chain migration. I think that needs to end. As far as the dock of the dreamers, I think, and I'm open to that, I think if we can solve these other issues, I don't think conservatives are opposed, right, to providing a pathway to citizenship. But to give them essentially a free pass and to tell them that they're going to jump ahead in line of all the folks that have done it legally, I don't think that's fair. I do think though that since they were brought here against, you know, they clearly were children when it happened. that they should have an opportunity to apply for citizenship and possibly have permanent status. But those problems can't be solved at the expense of a larger issue, which is our inability to protect our boundaries and our borders. That has to be handled first. And I think beyond that, simplification of the process, right, and then maybe refining the process to ensure that the people that are coming here have something to really offer our nation.
